entry.title: Concurrent, atomic MSI hash tables
entry.summary:
Readers will be familiar with Mask-Step-Index (MSI) hash tables, a technique for building fast, open-addressed hash tables in a dozen lines of code. If multiple threads or processes access an MSI table with at least one still inserting elements, care must be taken to avoid data races. This article will show how to add atomic operations to MSI tables in order to support different concurrency constraints. Let’s begin with the simplest case: An integer hash set, no deletions, only one insert thread (single producer), and consumers do not care about insert order. That is, the producer inserts A then B, but consumers may observe B in the table before A. Suppose this is the hash table in the single-threaded case:

entry.title: Traffic Premonitions
entry.summary: Exactly a year ago, an ambulance in Bangalore hit several people. The next day I was driving my scooter on the road besides an ambulance. The sight of the ambulance reminded me of the news story and I thought to myself, “it could happen to me, I should be careful.” We were stopped at a traffic signal, and I was lost in thoughts about the news. The signal turned green, we started moving, the ambulance took a sharp turn, and ran into me. Thankfully, both of us hit the brakes quite hard and the collision was minor. I got a severe whiplash from the sudden stop, and had to suffer through a backache for the next three months. entry.summary: The new w64devkit release two weeks ago is the first to be code-signed with my identity, verified by Microsoft’s certificate chain. Currently only the release packaging is signed — the self-extracting archive and its payload — but I will soon code-sign individual EXEs and DLLs within the distribution. My signing identity builds reputation with each download, so users will have an easier time with SmartScreen, and security software generally. We want to design fast algorithms, but when is an algorithm fast? Implement it, and measure the time.
Extrapolate experiments to predict performance on larger \(n\). May or may not give understanding. Does not provide lower bounds. Analyse exactly what happens on the CPU.
